newsitem.title: FRANCE: Europe leaves ECB questions unanswered.
newsitem.headline: Europe leaves ECB questions unanswered.

text.p: France's call for a euro-zone council to set policy under monetary union seems to be gathering support, but Europe faces an uphill task to define its role and crucially its relationship to the future European Central Bank.

While Paris and Bonn agree on the need for an informal body to co-ordinate policies after 1999, economists say differences in culture leave the division of power between the ECB and this council on exchange rate policy far from clear.

While Germany has traditionally left control of exchange rates to the Bundesbank, France has insisted managing the euro must remain in government hands, while the independent central bank is charged with maintaining price stability.

"I don't think it's going to be resolved. We have too much of a change (with monetary union) to be able to devise immediately the way the institutions will relate to each other," Bernard Godement, economist at Daiwa Institute of Research, said.
French and other officials have played down talk of a disagreement with Germany over the issue, insisting that Paris fully respects the need for an independent central bank.
"An independent central bank does not see any of its independence taken away if it talks to politicians," European affairs minister Michel Barnier told reporters last week.

"...the ECB and the governments in the euro zone must be able to talk to each other," Alexandre Lamfalussy, the Belgian head of the ECB's forerunner, the European Monetary Institute, said in an interview with French daily Liberation on Monday.
Officials say it is quite normal for the ECB and euro-zone governments to consult each other, just as the German government today talks to the Bundebank.

The question is how the two bodies relate to each other without impinging on commitments under the single-curency's guiding Maastricht treaty -- which forbids the ECB from taking advice from politicians, while also leaving governments with control of the external value of the euro.

Germany made an independent central bank committed to price stability a condition for accepting monetary union and France's determination to launch the euro on time appears to be strong enough for there to be little risk of it questioning this.

But some economists say, that facing record unemployment, it would probably have preferred a central bank more in line with the U.S. Federal Reserve, which must also take the health of the economy into account in pursuit of non-inflationary growth.
And that seems to be worrying the Bundesbank, which has launched a tirade on France's proposal for the stability council to act as a counterbalance to the ECB.
"It would be fatal to postpone such differences into the future as this could bring a rude awakening," Bundesbank council member Reimut Jochimsen said last week.
What will happen, for example, in the years to come if governments take a different view of inflation from the ECB?
"One of the problems of the Maastricht treaty is that it is timebound," Societe Generale economist Michala Marcussen said. "Everything is based on the current thinking of how best to ensure growth."

Another question is how to reconcile government control of the external value of the euro with central bank policies likely to look at both the internal and external value of the currency in determining inflation risk.
Officials say there will be much less risk of imported inflation from any devaluation in the euro, since most trade will be within the euro zone. That, however, will be for the ECB to judge.
And who will represent the euro-zone at international talks? France is unlikely, for example, to want to cede its place at the Group of Seven to a euro-zone representative.
But to resolve all such ambiguities, France would have to finesse a series of questions about how it sees Europe's future.

France has traditionally been very reluctant to adopt a German role model of a federal Europe, run by a European government. So in pushing a stability council, it has been careful to avoid suggestions it wants an economic government.
Godement said he did not think either France or Germany had a real interest in resolving ambiguities over the ECB.

French President Jacques Chirac needed people to believe monetary union would help tackle the problems of unemployment, while German Chancellor Helmut Kohl had to convince his people the mark would be as strong as the mark now is.
"I don't think anyone has an incentive to resolve it," Godement said. "Whatever is designed is likely to have to be revised in the light of developments."
